questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a 4 day history of fever, headache and feeling generally unwell. This morning his wife found him confused, struggling to find words, and he then had a generalised seizure. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg and GCS 12/15. There is no neck stiffness or rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever with altered mental state, dysphasia (temporal lobe) and new seizures after a flu-like illness is viral encephalitis, most often HSV.

steps.x: Febrile prodrome, then confusion, dysphasia and a seizure without meningism.

elim: Meningism would be expected; the main features here are confusion, dysphasia and seizures.
Usually follows a known source with focal signs evolving over longer.
Sudden thunderclap headache, not a febrile prodrome.
Causes headache and meningism without confusion, dysphasia or seizures.

steps.x: C: Herpes simplex encephalitis. Fever + confusion + seizure + focal signs = encephalitis (HSV until proven otherwise).

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman is admitted with 3 days of fever and headache. Today she has become disorientated and her partner says she complained of a strong smell of burning rubber that nobody else could smell. MRI brain shows bilateral temporal lobe high signal. CSF shows a lymphocytosis with normal glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: HSV, typically type 1, is the most common cause of viral encephalitis and classically involves the temporal lobes; olfactory hallucinations reflect temporal involvement.

steps.x: Temporal lobe signs and imaging with a viral CSF.

elim: Causes encephalitis mainly in severe immunosuppression.
Usually causes mild viral meningitis, not temporal lobe encephalitis.
Bacterial: neutrophils and low CSF glucose, with a rash.
A less common cause, usually after chickenpox or shingles.

steps.x: C: Herpes simplex virus type 1. Temporal lobe encephalitis = HSV-1.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman is brought in by her mother. She had a cold 3 weeks ago, then became anxious and sleepless, and over the last week she believes people are poisoning her. Today she had a seizure. She now has repetitive lip-licking movements and her pulse rate varies from 60 to 140 bpm. She has no psychiatric history.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young woman with psychiatric symptoms after a viral illness, then seizures, dyskinesia and autonomic instability has anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

steps.x: Young woman, post-viral psychosis, seizures, dyskinesia, autonomic swings.

elim: Seizures, abnormal movements and autonomic instability point to an organic cause.
No fever with meningism; course is over weeks.
Develops over days with fever; psychiatric prodrome over weeks favours autoimmune.
Does not cause autonomic instability and orofacial dyskinesia.

steps.x: B: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Young woman + new psychosis + seizures = anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has 2 months of worsening short-term memory; he cannot remember what he did that morning. His wife describes many daily episodes where he 'zones out' for a minute and does not respond. He has no fever. His MMSE score is 22/30 and CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Limbic encephalitis causes subacute short-term memory loss, confusion and seizures that appear as 'zoning out' absence-like episodes; in a smoker consider a paraneoplastic cause.

steps.x: Subacute memory loss with absence-like seizures in a smoker.

elim: A childhood epilepsy, not new in a 64 year old with memory loss.
Develops over years, not 2 months with seizures.
Acute with fever over days.
A single episode lasting hours, not repeated daily.

steps.x: D: Limbic encephalitis. Short-term memory loss + 'zoning out' seizures = limbic encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl had a routine vaccination 12 days ago. Over 2 days she has become drowsy and irritable, with an unsteady gait, weakness of the left leg and blurred vision. Her temperature is 37.8°C. MRI shows multiple patchy white matter lesions in the brain and spinal cord, all of the same age.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ADEM is a monophasic demyelinating illness after a viral infection or vaccination, with multifocal white matter lesions of the same age.

clues: unsteady gait, weakness of the left leg
steps.x: Multifocal demyelination soon after vaccination in a child.

elim: Does not cause multifocal white matter lesions.
Temporal lobe grey matter involvement, not widespread demyelination.
Lesions of different ages in an older patient; a single post-vaccine episode suggests ADEM.
Mild headache and meningism without focal deficits.

steps.x: A: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Post-infection/vaccine multifocal demyelination = ADEM.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has 2 days of fever and headache. Today he is confused and cannot name objects. On examination his neck is supple, Kernig's sign is negative and reflexes are brisk on the right with an upgoing right plantar. His temperature is 38.4°C and GCS 13/15.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Confusion and focal neurology without meningism, with brisk reflexes from CNS involvement, points to encephalitis rather than meningitis.

clues: reflexes are brisk on the right
steps.x: Fever with brain dysfunction and focal signs but no meningism.

elim: Causes headache and meningism but consciousness and higher function are preserved.
Does not cause fever and prolonged confusion.
No fever, confusion or focal signs.
Symptoms resolve within 24 hours and there is no fever.

steps.x: E: Viral encephalitis. Brain parenchyma involved (confusion, focal signs) = encephalitis, not meningitis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has fever, behavioural change and episodes of déjà vu for 3 days. Her temperature is 38.6°C and GCS 14/15. CSF shows a lymphocytosis and HSV PCR is awaited. IV aciclovir has been started.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI brain?
o: Dilated ventricles out of proportion to sulci
questions.e: HSV encephalitis classically involves the temporal lobes on MRI, often bilaterally.

steps.x: Temporal lobe symptoms with suspected HSV encephalitis.

elim: Normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Chronic Alzheimer's change.
Suggests abscesses or toxoplasmosis.
Multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: E: Temporal lobe high signal. HSV encephalitis on MRI: temporal lobe involvement.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman is admitted with 2 weeks of agitation, hallucinations and insomnia followed by seizures and reduced consciousness. CSF shows a mild lymphocytosis and anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are positive in CSF and serum. No pathogens are found.
questions.q: Which is the most likely associated finding on further investigation?
o: Small cell lung cancer on CT chest
questions.e: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in young women is often triggered by an ovarian teratoma expressing neural tissue, so pelvic imaging is needed.

steps.x: Confirmed anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman.

elim: Not the classic tumour association in a young woman.
Linked to other paraneoplastic syndromes, typical in older smokers.
Typical of HSV encephalitis.
Associated with myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: B: Ovarian teratoma on pelvic imaging. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: look for an ovarian teratoma.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has 3 days of fever and headache. His daughter says that today he is not himself: he is rude, keeps repeating questions and has forgotten her name. His temperature is 38.2°C. He is photophobic but his neck is not stiff. His GCS is 13/15.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests encephalitis rather than meningitis?
questions.e: Altered mental state, personality change and focal neurology indicate inflammation of the brain parenchyma itself (encephalitis); fever, headache and photophobia are shared with meningitis.

steps.x: Change in behaviour and memory without meningism.

elim: Occurs in both meningitis and encephalitis.
Occurs in both.
Not present here, and suggests meningeal involvement.
A feature of both.

steps.x: D: Personality change and confusion. Altered mental state or personality = brain parenchyma = encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student has had a flu-like illness for a week with high fevers. His flatmate found him confused this morning, then he had a seizure lasting 3 minutes. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and GCS 13/15. Reflexes are brisk throughout. He has no rash or neck stiffness and no previous seizures.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute viral encephalitis presents with altered mental status, high fevers and new-onset seizures, often after a flu-like illness.

steps.x: High fever, confusion and a first seizure after a flu-like illness.

elim: Occurs in young children, not a confused 19 year old.
Does not cause fever and persistent confusion.
Would cause a rash and shock.
Does not explain fever, brisk reflexes and persistent confusion.

steps.x: A: Acute viral encephalitis. Flu-like illness then confusion and new seizures = viral encephalitis.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman is brought in from home with 2 days of fever and increasing confusion. Her urine dipstick shows a trace of leucocytes only. She has a new expressive dysphasia and had a focal seizure of her right arm in the department. Her temperature is 38.7°C and GCS 12/15. CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Delirium due to urinary tract infection
questions.e: Fever with confusion, dysphasia and focal seizures in an older patient is encephalitis until proven otherwise; avoid anchoring on a trivial urine dipstick.

clues: focal seizure of her right arm
steps.x: Fever plus focal temporal and cortical signs in an elderly patient.

elim: A trace of leucocytes does not explain dysphasia and a focal seizure.
Does not cause fever with seizures and confusion.
A chronic triad, not an acute febrile illness.
CT head is normal.

steps.x: B: Herpes simplex encephalitis. Fever + focal neurology + seizure: think encephalitis, not just UTI delirium.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has fever, confusion and an olfactory aura before a seizure. He has been started on IV aciclovir. CT head is normal and a lumbar puncture has been done. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: CSF viral PCR, particularly HSV PCR, is the gold standard for viral encephalitis, confirming the virus and its subtype.

steps.x: Suspected HSV encephalitis with a lymphocytic CSF, raised protein and normal glucose.

elim: Identify bacteraemia, not a viral CNS infection.
Bacteria are unlikely with a lymphocytic CSF and normal glucose.
May show temporal changes but does not confirm the cause.
Shows past infection, which most adults have.

steps.x: C: CSF HSV PCR. Viral encephalitis gold standard: CSF PCR (HSV).

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 2 days of fever, headache and odd behaviour. Her GCS is 14/15 with no papilloedema or focal motor signs, and CT head is normal. IV aciclovir has been started. Full neurological examination has been completed.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: After a full neurological examination, lumbar puncture with CSF analysis is the first-line investigation for suspected encephalitis.

clues: Full neurological examination has been completed
steps.x: Suspected encephalitis with no contraindication to LP.

elim: Invasive and rarely needed.
For dementia with Lewy bodies.
Supportive but does not identify the cause.
Autoimmune testing does not replace CSF analysis.

steps.x: D: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis. Suspected encephalitis: examine, then LP with CSF analysis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has fever, confusion and a new seizure. He has had a sore throat and muscle aches for 4 days. His temperature is 38.5°C and GCS 14/15. CT head is normal and lumbar puncture is performed. He is started on IV aciclovir. His opening pressure is mildly raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of CSF results?
o: India ink positive yeasts, low glucose
Normal cells, normal protein, normal glucose
questions.e: Viral encephalitis gives a lymphocytosis with raised protein and normal glucose.

clues: fever, confusion and a new seizure
steps.x: Suspected viral encephalitis.

elim: Cryptococcal meningitis in the immunocompromised.
Bacterial meningitis.
Would argue against an infective encephalitis.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: B: Lymphocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose. Viral CSF: lymphocytes, raised protein, normal glucose.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has 2 weeks of paranoid delusions, insomnia and agitation followed by two seizures. She has had no fever. CSF shows a mild lymphocytosis with normal glucose, and CSF HSV PCR is negative. MRI brain is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: CSF and serum anti-NMDA receptor antibodies
questions.e: Autoimmune encephalitis is confirmed by antibody testing in CSF and serum, such as anti-NMDA receptor antibodies.

steps.x: Psychosis and seizures in a young woman with a bland CSF and negative viral PCR.

elim: Not specific for this picture.
HSV is already excluded and the picture is autoimmune.
Linked to Hashimoto's encephalopathy, a rare alternative.
May be useful but cannot confirm encephalitis.

steps.x: B: CSF and serum anti-NMDA receptor antibodies. Autoimmune encephalitis gold standard: antibody testing.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has 3 weeks of agitation, hallucinations and abnormal movements of her mouth, then seizures. She had a viral illness a month ago. Her temperature is 37.4°C. Lumbar puncture is performed and anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CSF analysis?
o: Mild lymphocytosis with no organism identified
questions.e: Autoimmune encephalitis typically gives a mild lymphocytosis with no pathogen identified; the diagnosis rests on autoantibodies.

steps.x: Post-viral psychosis, dyskinesia and seizures: autoimmune encephalitis.

elim: Meningococcal meningitis.
Cryptococcal meningitis.
Bacterial meningitis.
Viral HSV encephalitis, not autoimmune.

steps.x: D: Mild lymphocytosis with no organism identified. Autoimmune encephalitis CSF: mild lymphocytosis, no pathogen.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has fever, confusion and a seizure. He is on IV aciclovir. His CT head is normal and CSF shows a lymphocytosis but the HSV PCR result will take 2 days. The team want imaging that best shows parenchymal involvement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
questions.e: MRI brain is the second-line imaging for encephalitis and shows temporal lobe involvement, particularly in HSV encephalitis, often when CT is normal.

steps.x: Suspected encephalitis with a normal CT.

elim: For stroke risk assessment.
For aneurysms or vessel occlusion.
For parkinsonian syndromes.
Much less sensitive than MRI for early encephalitis.

steps.x: D: MRI brain. Imaging of choice in encephalitis: MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 3 day history of fever and headache, and today she is confused and has had a seizure. Her temperature is 38.8°C and GCS 13/15. There is no neck stiffness or rash. CT head is normal and lumbar puncture has just been performed. The CSF results will take 1 hour.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Wait for CSF results before treating
Wait for HSV PCR before treating
questions.e: Suspected viral encephalitis is treated with high-dose IV aciclovir immediately without waiting for confirmatory results.

clues: confused and has had a seizure
The CSF results will take 1 hour
steps.x: Suspected encephalitis with results pending.

elim: Too little reaches the CNS; IV high-dose is needed.
For autoimmune encephalitis once confirmed.
Never wait: untreated HSV encephalitis has high mortality.
PCR takes days; delay worsens necrosis.

steps.x: B: Start high-dose IV aciclovir now. Suspected encephalitis: IV aciclovir now, do not wait.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a 1 day history of fever, headache and neck stiffness, and has become confused and drowsy. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg. Kernig's sign is positive. Blood cultures have been taken. He has no drug allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV ceftriaxone, IV aciclovir and IV amoxicillin
questions.e: An overlapping meningitis and encephalitis picture is treated empirically for both with IV ceftriaxone and IV aciclovir, adding IV amoxicillin over 60 to cover Listeria.

steps.x: Meningism and confusion in a patient over 60.

elim: Does not cover bacterial meningitis.
Covers Listeria only, not HSV or most meningitis organisms.
Does not cover HSV encephalitis or Listeria.
Misses Listeria cover needed over 60.

steps.x: E: IV ceftriaxone, IV aciclovir and IV amoxicillin. Meningoencephalitis over 60: ceftriaxone + aciclovir + amoxicillin.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has 1 day of fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. Over the last 3 hours she has become confused and her husband says she is talking nonsense. Her temperature is 39.0°C and GCS 13/15. There is no rash. Blood cultures have been taken and she has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV ceftriaxone, IV aciclovir and IV amoxicillin
questions.e: Meningism with confusion suggests both meningitis and encephalitis, so both are treated empirically with IV ceftriaxone and IV aciclovir.

steps.x: Meningism plus altered mental state in a young adult.

elim: Leaves bacterial meningitis untreated.
Neither covers HSV nor is the first choice in hospital.
Misses HSV encephalitis.
Listeria cover is only added over 60, under 3 months or in pregnancy.

steps.x: D: IV ceftriaxone and IV aciclovir. Overlap picture under 60: ceftriaxone + aciclovir.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis confirmed by CSF antibodies. She has seizures and orofacial dyskinesia. Pelvic MRI shows a right ovarian teratoma. Her HSV PCR is negative. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 150/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV methylprednisolone and IVIg with removal of the teratoma
questions.e: First-line treatment of autoimmune encephalitis is IV methylprednisolone and IVIg, with removal of any teratoma and plasma exchange as an adjunct.

steps.x: Confirmed autoimmune encephalitis with a tumour trigger.

elim: HSV is excluded; this is autoimmune.
Inadequate first-line immunotherapy.
Second-line, after no response to first-line therapy.
Immunotherapy is needed as well.

steps.x: B: IV methylprednisolone and IVIg with removal of the teratoma. Anti-NMDAR: steroids + IVIg + remove teratoma.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has autoimmune encephalitis with positive anti-LGI1 antibodies and no tumour on screening. He received IV methylprednisolone, IVIg and plasma exchange. Two weeks later he is still having daily seizures and his memory has not improved.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If there is no response to first-line immunotherapy within 2 weeks, second-line treatment is rituximab and cyclophosphamide.

steps.x: First-line immunotherapy has failed after 2 weeks.

elim: No viral cause; this is antibody-mediated.
Not the next step for autoimmune encephalitis.
A step down, not escalation.
Escalation to second-line agents is needed.

steps.x: E: Rituximab and cyclophosphamide. No response by 2 weeks: rituximab and cyclophosphamide.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with HSV encephalitis is on day 2 of IV aciclovir. He has had three seizures in an hour without full recovery between them, his GCS has fallen to 8/15 and he is struggling to protect his airway. His oxygen saturation is 89% on 15 L oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Admit to ICU for airway support and seizure control
Transfer to a general medical ward
questions.e: Encephalitis needs supportive care: seizure control and ICU admission when consciousness or the airway is compromised.

steps.x: Seizures, low GCS and failing airway.

elim: The cause is known; the problem is airway and seizures.
Unsafe with falling GCS and does not help now.
Aciclovir must continue.
He needs critical care.

steps.x: B: Admit to ICU for airway support and seizure control. Supportive care: control seizures, ICU if needed.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with suspected viral encephalitis is waiting for a lumbar puncture, which is delayed until the next morning. A junior doctor suggests holding off antiviral treatment until the HSV PCR is back to avoid unnecessary drugs.
questions.q: Which is the strongest reason to start IV aciclovir now?
o: Aciclovir is needed to make the PCR positive
Aciclovir reduces the risk of a teratoma
HSV PCR is unreliable after 24 hours
Untreated HSV causes haemorrhagic necrosis with high mortality
questions.e: HSV encephalitis causes haemorrhagic necrosis, so untreated disease has high mortality and aciclovir starts immediately, before CSF results.

steps.x: Delay to treatment in suspected HSV encephalitis.

elim: Treatment does not help the test.
It has no antibacterial activity.
Irrelevant to viral encephalitis.
The reason to treat is the disease, not the test.

steps.x: E: Untreated HSV causes haemorrhagic necrosis with high mortality. Do not wait: HSV causes haemorrhagic necrosis.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with recurrent cold sores develops fever, confusion and a smell of burning that nobody else notices. MRI shows high signal in both temporal lobes and the orbitofrontal cortex. HSV-1 PCR is positive in his CSF.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the distribution of brain involvement?
o: Direct spread from an infected middle ear
Reactivation with retrograde spread along trigeminal and olfactory pathways
questions.e: HSV encephalitis involves the temporal and frontal lobes because of viral reactivation and retrograde spread along trigeminal and olfactory pathways.

clues: both temporal lobes and the orbitofrontal cortex
steps.x: HSV with temporal and frontal involvement.

elim: Would not cause selective temporal involvement.
Causes abscess, not temporal encephalitis.
Would give meningitis, not focal temporal disease.
Molecular mimicry in ADEM.

steps.x: E: Reactivation with retrograde spread along trigeminal and olfactory pathways. HSV reaches temporal/frontal lobes via trigeminal and olfactory nerves.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman has psychosis, seizures and orofacial dyskinesia. CSF shows a mild lymphocytosis and HSV PCR is negative. An ovarian teratoma is found and removed. A medical student asks what the antibodies in her CSF are targeting.
questions.q: Which is the most likely target of the antibodies?
o: Acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor
questions.e: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is mediated by autoantibodies against the NR1 subunit, often triggered by an ovarian teratoma containing neural tissue.

steps.x: Teratoma-linked psychosis and seizures in a young woman.

elim: Myasthenia gravis.
Not the target in this classic syndrome.
Linked to limbic encephalitis, not this teratoma syndrome.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

steps.x: C: NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis: antibodies to the NR1 subunit.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy had measles 2 weeks ago. He now has drowsiness, ataxia and weakness of both legs. MRI shows widespread white matter lesions in the brain and spinal cord. CSF has a mild lymphocytosis and viral PCR is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his illness?
o: Molecular mimicry with immune cross-reaction against myelin
questions.e: ADEM follows infection or vaccination when the immune response cross-reacts with myelin antigens (molecular mimicry).

steps.x: Post-infectious multifocal demyelination.

elim: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis causes psychosis and dyskinesia, not demyelination.
No bacterial infection.
Viral PCR is negative; this is post-infectious.
Causes slowly progressive CJD.

steps.x: D: Molecular mimicry with immune cross-reaction against myelin. ADEM = molecular mimicry against myelin.
